Flood can have a low humanitarian impact based on the magnitude, exposed population and vulnerability. At least 20 people were killed, around 80 others injured, and more than 100 remain missing, in Nuristan Province following flash floods triggered by heavy rainfall.

UN News (22 July 2026): flash floods triggered by heavy rainfall on 20 July have killed at least 26 people across eastern Afghanistan, including 23 in Nuristan province, where homes, markets and roads were swept away, with the worst devastation in Parun City (7 houses completely destroyed, 23 partially damaged, 70 shops and 11 hotels damaged, 40 vehicles lost). The floods also killed three Afghan refugees at a returnee transit camp near the Torkham border crossing with Pakistan and injured nine others there. OCHA said the immediate priority is to save lives and reach people who may still be missing or injured, and warned that casualty figures could rise as more information becomes available; UNICEF and partners are setting up a field clinic in Parun for trauma care.

OCHA Flash Update #2: Flooding in Eastern Afghanistan (22-23 July 2026): in Parun City, Nuristan Province, local authorities report 23 killed, 5 missing (down from over 100) and 125 injured (38 severe, 87 minor). At the Torkham transit camp in Nangarhar, 3 Afghan refugees were killed and 9 injured (unchanged). One additional death is reported in Maidan Wardak province (Sayedabad District). The response has moved from immediate search and rescue and emergency life-saving assistance towards a broader, multi-sector response addressing shelter, health, food, WASH, protection, livelihoods and planning to address early recovery needs.

OCHA Flash Update #3: Flooding in Central, Eastern and Southeastern Afghanistan (as of 28 July 2026): in Laghman Province, three people were killed and four others injured, with 187 families affected and 183 houses damaged or destroyed; approximately 800 acres of seasonal crops and around 310 livestock were also reportedly lost or damaged. Nuristan Province remains the most severely affected area; the completed inter-agency needs assessment in Parun district identified 120 families eligible for humanitarian assistance, of which the first 92 have already received assistance. The Shelter/NFI cluster reports 1,168 families have been affected across 14 provinces, including 234 houses completely destroyed and 930 houses damaged. Needs assessments in Maidan Wardak and Panjshir are expected to commence shortly.

This WHO cumulative figure reflects domestic flood-affected provinces only and does not include the 3 Afghan refugees killed at the Torkham border transit camp that OCHA's Flash Update series counted toward the combined 30-death toll already on file; the two figures use different scopes and neither supersedes the other.

claims.text: GDACS's event report for a Green-alert forest fire in Algeria (18-22 July 2026 window, Seraidi/Constantine area) cites about 11,362 hectares burned and roughly 2,870 people exposed. Algeria's interior ministry reported six deaths from the wildfires, and authorities reported more than 100 people hospitalised in the town of Seraidi and about 150 homes damaged there.

GDACS's event report for a second concurrent Green-alert forest fire in Algeria, now at episode 6 covering an 18-24 July 2026 window, cites about 14,082 hectares burned. Algeria's interior ministry registered six deaths in relation to the fires affecting multiple provinces during this period; four people were arrested on suspicion of deliberately starting fires.

GDACS's event report for a third concurrent Green-alert forest fire in Algeria, now at episode 5 covering a 21-24 July 2026 window, cites about 13,388 hectares burned, assessed as low humanitarian impact based on burned area and affected population. Thermal-anomaly detections continue to be recorded as of 24 July 2026.

Over the last 24 hours, the Ministry of the Interior, Local Authorities and Transport confirmed six fatalities linked to the wildfires. In Seraïdi, Annaba, more than 100 patients were evacuated from a rehabilitation hospital, while approximately 150 homes were affected or threatened. Preventive evacuations were also carried out in several localities, including El Tarf, Béjaïa, Guelma and Bouira.

GDACS event report (eventid 1029625, episode 8): Algeria wildfire complex covering an 18-25 July 2026 window, citing about 11,864 hectares burned, with the most recent satellite thermal-anomaly detection recorded on 25 July 2026 and no further detections after the window closed.

GDACS event report (eventid 1029611, episode 6): Algeria wildfire complex covering an 18-24 July 2026 window, citing about 14,082 hectares burned, with the most recent satellite thermal-anomaly detection recorded on 24 July 2026 and no further detections since.

GDACS event report (eventid 1029618, episode 8): Algeria wildfire complex covering a 21-24 July 2026 window, citing about 13,459 hectares burned, with the most recent satellite thermal-anomaly detection recorded on 24 July 2026 and no further detections since.

Re-checked 1 August 2026: GDACS's event report for the Seraïdi/Constantine complex (eventid 1029625) has advanced to episode 10, citing about 11,942 hectares burned and roughly 1,210 people in the affected area, with the last thermal-anomaly detection still 25 July 2026 and the alert level downgraded to Green. The other two complexes (eventid 1029611: 14,082 ha/5,885 people, last detection 24 July; eventid 1029618: 13,459 ha/147 people, last detection 24 July) are unchanged from the prior check, confirming no further escalation.

published.description: A wave of wildfires swept northern Algeria's forested provinces (including Constantine and Seraïdi) from mid-to-late July 2026 amid a severe regional heatwave, with GDACS tracking three concurrent Green-alert fire complexes that together burned roughly 39,400 hectares. Algeria's interior ministry confirmed six deaths and authorities reported over 100 people hospitalised and about 150 homes damaged in the Seraïdi area, with preventive evacuations also carried out in El Tarf, Béjaïa, Guelma and Bouira; four people were arrested on suspicion of deliberately starting fires. As of 24-25 July 2026, GDACS records no further satellite thermal-anomaly detections for any of the three complexes, and Algerian civil protection authorities describe the blazes as under control.

impact.summary: GDACS's three concurrent Algeria wildfire complexes closed out at a combined ~39,483 hectares burned: the Seraïdi/Constantine complex (GDACS event 1029625, now episode 10) at 11,942 ha with about 1,210 people in the affected area and its final thermal-anomaly detection on 25 July, and the alert level for this complex has since downgraded to Green; a second complex (event 1029611, episode 6) at 14,082 ha with about 5,885 people affected, last detection 24 July; and a third (event 1029618, episode 8) at 13,459 ha with about 147 people affected, last detection 24 July. Algeria's interior ministry confirmed six deaths from the fires (unchanged since 22 July), and a 22 July Algerian Red Crescent/IFRC report via ReliefWeb put more than 100 people hospitalised and about 150 homes affected or threatened in Seraïdi, Annaba, with preventive evacuations also carried out in El Tarf, Béjaïa, Guelma and Bouira. Re-checked 1 August 2026: no new thermal detections have been recorded for any of the three complexes since 24-25 July, and Algerian civil protection authorities continue to describe the blazes as under control, confirming the event remains contained.

At least 59 people have died nationwide (up from 53/51). In Cox's Bazar's 33 Rohingya refugee camps, flooding/landslides affected 28,000+ people, damaged 3,100+ shelters, and displaced 4,700+ individuals; UNHCR has confirmed 15 deaths among Rohingya refugees. As of 16 July only the Kushiyara River remained above danger level (at Markuli, Sunamganj and Fenchuganj, Sylhet), and water levels in the Surma (Sylhet/Sunamganj) and the Teesta, Dharla and Dudhkumar rivers (Rangpur Division) were falling.

Bangladesh Red Crescent Society Situation Report 4: Monsoon Flood & Landslide Response (posted 20 Jul 2026, originally published 17 Jul 2026), covering Chattogram, Cox's Bazar, Bandarban, Rangamati, Khagrachhari, Cumilla, Moulvibazar, Habiganj, Sunamganj and Sylhet. As of 16 July 9:00 AM, only the Kushiyara River remained above danger level (Markuli/Sunamganj and Fenchuganj/Sylhet stations); the Someshwari River at Kalmakanda had receded below danger level; Surma river conditions in Sylhet/Sunamganj were expected to improve within 24 hours; Teesta, Dharla and Dudhkumar river levels in Rangpur Division were falling and projected to fall further. published.description: Belgium's largest wildfire on record broke out on 14 August 2026 in the Hautes Fagnes (High Fens) nature reserve in eastern Belgium's Liege province, near the German border, during a prolonged drought and heat spell. GDACS recorded the fire (event 1030534) burning 6,356 hectares over three days (14-17 August 2026) with 119 people exposed within the burned area, assessing an overall alert level of 1.5 -- 'no humanitarian impact' by its burned-area/population formula, reflecting the reserve's sparse population rather than the fire's true scale, which international media and Belgian officials described as the country's largest wildfire on record / worst in a century. Belgium activated the EU Civil Protection Mechanism (UCPM); the European Commission's civil protection service reports that 2 rescEU firefighting planes were dispatched from Sweden and firefighting helicopters were sent from the Netherlands, Norway and Germany to support local crews battling the blaze, with the EU's Copernicus Emergency Management Service activated to provide rapid mapping. The fire prompted evacuation orders in the towns of Waimes and Butgenbach and threatened to cross into Germany near Monschau before rain and firefighting efforts halted its advance.

impact.summary: GDACS's report for this event (WF 1030534, 14-17 August 2026) records 6,356 hectares burned and 119 people exposed within the burned area, assessing an overall alert level of 1.5 ('no humanitarian impact' by its burned-area/population formula). published.description: A fast-moving wildfire outbreak swept British Columbia's Interior in early August 2026, led by the Bald Range fire, which was first reported the evening of 7 August 2026 near Summerland in the South Okanagan and grew rapidly overnight, prompting a full evacuation order for the roughly 12,000 residents of the District of Summerland. On 8 August 2026, BC's Minister of Emergency Management and Climate Readiness, Kelly Greene, declared a provincewide State of Provincial Emergency, citing the addition of the fast-moving Bald Range fire and the large-scale overnight evacuation. GDACS assessed the wildfire situation in Canada (event 1030240) as an overall Green alert for low humanitarian impact, recording a burned area of 13,006 hectares and about 4,746 people affected in the burned area for the 8-11 August reporting window -- a snapshot that understates the province-wide response, since it covers only the tracked episode window and GDACS itself flags this as a low-impact rating. The BC government's own emergency-information channels confirm the state of emergency remains active, and the provincial government has begun deploying support resources, including more than 1,000 hotel rooms and nearly 1,000 group-lodging beds in the Okanagan for evacuees, mobile ServiceBC units in Penticton and Kelowna, and a twenty-fold increase in BC Evacuee Helpline staffing capacity. On 9 August 2026, Penticton RCMP confirmed the province's first wildfire-related fatality: an 80-year-old Meadow Valley resident who died suddenly while attempting to evacuate with a family member as the Bald Range fire swept through; RCMP said they believe the death resulted from the wildfire, with the BC Coroners Service investigating to confirm the cause of death. No allowlisted source has declared the state of emergency lifted or the fires contained. claims.text: USGS recorded a magnitude 7.4 earthquake on 10 August 2026 at 12:34:28 UTC, located 5 km S of San José del Palmar, Colombia (4.8436°N, -76.2422°W) at a depth of 110.3 km. USGS's PAGER system assessed an Orange alert level, with approximately 10.5 million people exposed to Strong-to-Very-Strong (MMI VI+) shaking.

Re-checked 12 August 2026: GDACS's earthquake report for this event (event id 1557236, episode 1724218) has escalated to an Overall Red alert for high humanitarian impact, with a GDACS score of 2.2 (up from 1.7) and about 5.2 million people now within zones of MMI VII or greater shaking (up from about 1.5 million). The page's casualty line, citing media reports and not independently verified by GDACS, now reads 'at least 240 deaths' -- higher than, and not adopted in place of, the government-sourced UN News figure below.

UN News (11 August 2026), 'Colombia earthquake: UN joins national response': citing Colombia's president, 'more than 180 have died' and 'hundreds have been injured'; 'nearly 5,000 homes have been damaged and 387 have been destroyed'; '61 buildings have collapsed'; 'more than 550 educational institutions, 24 health facilities and more than 350 community centres have [been] affected'; the government has activated emergency coordination centres in Bogotá, Quibdó, Armenia and Cali and has requested UN support.

Servicio Geológico Colombiano (10 August 2026): confirms the magnitude 7.4 event centered near San José del Palmar at a depth of about 103 km, recorded 18 aftershocks (magnitude 1.4-4.8) as of midday 10 August, describes it as 'the seismic event of greatest magnitude recorded in Colombia in the 21st century,' and notes more than 12,000 people from 900 populated centres reported feeling the earthquake. The bulletin gives no casualty figures.

USGS's PAGER alert for the earthquake (event us6000tjl2) escalated to Red as of 13 August 2026 06:30:47 UTC (magnitude 7.4, MMI 7.999, CDI 7.9, 1,121 felt reports), up from the Orange level recorded 11 August 2026.

OCHA Colombia's Flash Update 004 (posted 13 August 2026, data as of 12 August 18:30 local time): 'The emergency continues to escalate and has exceeded the local response capacity, with at least 49,214 people affected, 30,324 families impacted, 3,771 injured people, and 241 fatalities across 13 departments of the country... Damage to more than 54,900 homes (destroyed and damaged)... the USD 5 million CERF allocation represents a critical boost to scale up the emergency response.'

OCHA Colombia, Flash Update 005 (as of 13 August, 18:30 local time): "The scale of the emergency continues to grow. Heavy rainfall and related impacts have affected 53,816 people (25,872 families) across at least 13 departments and 401 municipalities nationwide, including 266 deaths and 11,789 homes destroyed. The most affected departments are Risaralda, Valle del Cauca, Chocó and Caldas. However, the emergency continues to expand and figures may increase due to access constraints and possible underreporting."

OCHA Colombia's Flash Update No. 006 (data as of 14 August 2026, 18:30 local time): 287 deaths, 3,975 injured, 378 missing, 135,179 affected people (56,448 affected families) across 15 departments and 437 municipalities, 13,077 homes destroyed; 183 aftershocks have followed the mainshock (15 of magnitude >3, two >4); an initial US$5 million CERF allocation is supporting the response.

published.description: A magnitude 7.4 intermediate-depth earthquake struck western Colombia on 10 August 2026 at 12:34:28 UTC, centered 5 km S of San José del Palmar in Chocó Department, about 240 km west of Bogotá, at a depth of roughly 110 km. USGS's PAGER system assessed an Orange alert level, with an estimated 10.5 million people exposed to strong-to-very-strong shaking (MMI VI+). GDACS initially assessed the event as an Orange alert for medium humanitarian impact; re-checked 12 August 2026, GDACS has escalated the event to a Red alert for high humanitarian impact, with its score rising from 1.7 to 2.2 and its population-exposure estimate for MMI VII+ shaking rising from about 1.5 million to about 5.2 million. UN News (11 August 2026) reports that Colombia's government has confirmed 'more than 180' deaths, hundreds injured, nearly 5,000 homes damaged (387 destroyed), 61 buildings collapsed, and more than 550 educational institutions, 24 health facilities and 350 community centres affected; the government has activated emergency coordination centres in Bogotá, Quibdó, Armenia and Cali and requested UN support. Colombia's national geological survey (SGC) recorded 18 aftershocks (M1.4-4.8) as of midday 10 August and described the mainshock as the strongest recorded in Colombia in the 21st century. Bogotá's own emergency-management office (IDIGER) inspected nearly 4,800 homes/offices in the capital and found no moderate or severe structural damage there, indicating the worst damage is concentrated in Chocó, Valle del Cauca, Caldas and Risaralda rather than the capital. Colombian news media have reported that President Abelardo De la Espriella signed a national-disaster decree; this decree itself remains unconfirmed by a directly-fetched allowlisted source, though UN News does confirm the government has activated emergency coordination centres. OCHA Colombia's Flash Update 004 (12 August 2026) reports the emergency 'continues to escalate and has exceeded the local response capacity,' with the confirmed toll rising to 241 deaths, 3,771 injured, 49,214 people affected and 30,324 families impacted across 13 departments, and damage to more than 54,900 homes; USGS's PAGER alert was raised from Orange to Red the same day (magnitude 7.4, 1,121 felt reports). Re-checked 14 August 2026: OCHA Colombia's Flash Update 005 (posted 14 August 2026, data as of 13 August 18:30 local time) reports 266 deaths and 53,816 people (25,872 families) affected across 13 departments and 401 municipalities, with 11,789 homes destroyed — up from 241 deaths and 49,214 people affected in Flash Update 004. USGS and GDACS alert levels remain Red, unchanged. Re-checked 15 August 2026: OCHA Colombia's Flash Update 006 (posted 15 August 2026, data as of 14 August 18:30 local time) reports the affected population has risen sharply to at least 135,179 people across 15 departments (up from 13) and 437 municipalities (up from 401), with 183 aftershocks recorded five days after the mainshock and an initial US$5 million CERF allocation supporting the international response; the report gives no updated death toll or homes-destroyed figure in its accessible summary text. GDACS's report page (still Red alert) carries a media-echo citation from Italian outlet ITALPRESS of "at least 281 deaths and 3,900 injured," attributed to third-party media rather than to GDACS's own assessment, USGS, or OCHA; this figure is not adopted and the confirmed toll remains 266 deaths per OCHA Flash Update 005 (13 August). claims.text: On 17 May 2026 the WHO Director-General determined that the epidemic of Ebola disease caused by Bundibugyo virus in the DRC and Uganda constitutes a Public Health Emergency of International Concern (PHEIC).

WHO Disease Outbreak News #613 (17 July 2026): as of 15 July 2026, the Democratic Republic of the Congo reported 2,124 confirmed cases including 828 deaths (case fatality ratio 39%), with Ituri province the most affected (27 of 36 health zones; 89.6% of cases, 83.6% of deaths), and further cases in North Kivu (11 of 34 health zones), South Kivu (1 of 34 health zones), Haut-Uele (4 of 13 health zones) and Tshopo (3 of 23 health zones). As of 17 July 2026, Uganda reported 20 confirmed cases including two deaths in imported cases plus one probable case resulting in death. WHO assessed the risk as very high nationally in DRC due to ongoing transmission and expansion into new health zones, high in Uganda due to confirmed cross-border spread, high for countries sharing land borders with the affected countries, and low for the rest of the African region and globally.

Page last updated 21 July 2026, 17:00. On 20 July 2026 (data up until 19 July), the Democratic Republic of the Congo reported a total of 2,423 confirmed cases including 967 related deaths, an increase of 79 new confirmed cases and 37 deaths since the previous update; 734 patients are hospitalised in isolation and 469 have recovered. Ituri province remains the most affected, with 2,160 cases including 811 deaths, reported from 28 of 36 health zones (up from 27/36); North Kivu has reported 239 cases including 141 deaths from 11 of 34 health zones; South Kivu 3 cases including 1 death from 1 of 34 health zones; Haut-Uele 16 cases including 10 deaths from 4 of 13 health zones; and Tshopo 5 cases including 4 deaths from 3 of 23 health zones — 47 of 140 health zones affected in total, still across the same five provinces (no new province reported). Uganda has reported 20 confirmed cases including two deaths, with the last confirmed case on 21 June and no new cases since; its last patient was discharged on 16 July, and the 42-day countdown toward declaring Uganda's outbreak over is ongoing.

claims.text: In the space of just three weeks, the UN Human Rights Office documented 15 drone strikes on El Obeid, which killed at least 45 civilians. El Obeid has more than half a million residents, together with at least 100,000 internally displaced persons, and the number of newly displaced people across Kordofan has risen by nearly two-thirds in only three months.

Re-checked 3 August 2026: a search of reliefweb.int and news.un.org found no new aggregate death toll or IDP figure specific to El Obeid beyond those already cited; siege and drone-strike conditions continue with no ceasefire or ground assault reported.

UN News (3 August 2026), citing OCHA: renewed drone attacks in recent days in El Obeid, capital of North Kordofan state, have put civilians, critical infrastructure and humanitarian operations at risk. UN Emergency Relief Coordinator Tom Fletcher said humanitarians are scaling up efforts to reach families hit by conflict in North Kordofan and will seize every opening to expand lifesaving aid in and around El Obeid. OCHA noted that approximately $1.2 billion of the $2.9 billion required for Sudan's 2026 humanitarian response had been received. No new aggregate death toll or IDP figure specific to El Obeid was published in this update.

UN News (3 August 2026), citing OCHA: 'Renewed drone attacks in recent days in El Obeid ... have also put civilians, critical infrastructure and humanitarian operations at risk.' No new aggregate death toll or IDP figure specific to El Obeid has been published beyond the 3 July UN Human Rights Office count (45+ killed) and the 17 July WFP camp-population figure (120,000+).

Re-checked 7 August 2026 via direct fetch of reliefweb.int/country/sdn: no El-Obeid-specific aggregate death toll or IDP figure has been published beyond the 3 July 2026 UN Human Rights Office count (45+ killed) and the 17 July 2026 WFP camp-population figure (120,000+); the most recent El-Obeid-specific ReliefWeb item remains a 31 July 2026 Plan International piece on cholera risk, with no new casualty/IDP numbers.

Re-checked 8 August 2026: UN News (3 August 2026) reports renewed drone strikes threatening civilians and aid operations in El Obeid but gives no new aggregate death toll or IDP count; ReliefWeb's Sudan country page shows no new El-Obeid-specific casualty/IDP figures beyond what's already cited (45+ deaths, UN Human Rights Office 3 July; 120,000+ IDPs, WFP 17 July).

UN News (3 August 2026), citing OCHA, reports renewed drone attacks in recent days in El Obeid threatening civilians, infrastructure and humanitarian operations, and cites more than 100,000 displaced people sheltering in camps in the city — a figure of different scope from WFP's 17 July count of 120,000+ in the Unified IDP Camp alone. No new aggregate death toll specific to El Obeid has been published beyond the 3 July UN Human Rights Office count (at least 45 civilians killed).

UN News (10 August 2026), citing OCHA: RSF forces have encircled El Obeid, capital of North Kordofan, threatening a full-scale ground assault as civilians flock to the city and surrounding areas in search of safety and assistance. Humanitarian partners delivered two million litres of drinking water to about 133,000 people amid severe water shortages. The UN Secretary-General's Personal Envoy has held meetings with both sides and is working toward a full cessation of hostilities. No new aggregate death toll or IDP figure specific to El Obeid was published in this update, beyond the 3 July UN Human Rights Office count (45+ killed) and the 17 July WFP camp-population figure (120,000+).

Re-checked 12 August 2026: UN News's most recent Sudan article (10 August 2026, on the RSF encirclement of El Obeid) remains the latest allowlisted report on this event; no article dated after 10 August with new El-Obeid-specific figures was found. No death toll newer than the 3 July UN Human Rights Office figure (at least 45 civilians killed) and no IDP figure newer than WFP's 17 July figure (120,000+ in the Unified IDP Camp alone) has been published.

UN News (12 August 2026), citing OCHA: 'Multiple waves of drone strikes were reported on Wednesday across El Obeid, the North Kordofan capital'... 'roughly 15,000 families have been displaced to El Obeid over the past three weeks,' driven by continuing attacks and insecurity in northern parts of the state, with OCHA noting the influx is 'putting greater pressure on displacement sites and basic services that are already overstretched.' This is a new inflow-displacement figure, distinct in scope from the existing cumulative death toll (45+ killed, UN Human Rights Office, 3 July 2026) and the Unified IDP Camp population figure (120,000+, WFP, 17 July 2026); no new aggregate death toll specific to El Obeid was reported.

Save the Children, via ReliefWeb (14 August 2026): "Nearly 39,000 children fled to the city of El Obeid in North Kordofan, Sudan, over the first six months of the year, escaping violence and attacks on civilians and civilian infrastructure that have uprooted families across the state... The new arrivals are now part of more than 605,000 people living in El Obeid town and Sheikan locality... In April 2026, Save the Children-supported health facilities in Sheikan locality treated 426 children for malnutrition, compared with 195 in March, marking a 118% month-on-month increase... individual [water] consumption has now been reduced to approximately 7 litres per person per day, less than half of the general minimum standard of 15 litres recommended by the World Health Organization during crises."

G7 Foreign Ministers' joint statement on El Obeid, Sudan (14 July 2026): condemns ongoing RSF drone strikes on El Obeid and obstruction of humanitarian access, references the precedent of atrocities in El Fasher, and calls for an immediate ceasefire and compliance with the Jeddah Declaration to protect civilians.

UN News (10 August 2026): RSF drone attacks continue on El Obeid, capital of North Kordofan, even as the UN and partners have provided two million litres of drinking water to about 133,000 people amid severe water shortages; separately, 18,000 people were displaced from over 20 villages in West Darfur in the preceding week, and 75,000 displaced persons were cut off from care after three health facilities closed in Central Darfur. Sudan-wide, more than 30 million people need assistance, over 9 million are internally displaced, and the US$3 billion humanitarian appeal is only about 40% funded (US$1.2 billion received).

NRC report (posted 7 July 2026) on El Obeid: families are dying from drone strikes and from hunger as the siege continues, with an aid convoy struck the preceding week; essential services and food access are collapsing further as the blockade persists.

UN News (17 July 2026): the UN human rights chief warned that civilians in El Obeid "have been under siege for 18 months" and face continuous drone strikes, with more than 100,000 displaced people sheltering in camps in the city. WFP is providing food assistance to over 100,000 people in those camps, including nutrition support for 17,000 children, but is distributing only a reduced ration that recipients are sharing with other families. Almost 20 million people in Sudan are now classified as acutely food insecure, and more than 14 million people have been uprooted nationwide since the conflict began.

WFP Geneva Palais briefing note (published 17 July 2026): El Obeid city (population approximately 500,000) is hosting displaced people, with more than 120,000 people in the 'Unified IDP Camp' alone. WFP is providing food/cash assistance to just over 100,000 people in camps inside the city, but severe funding shortfalls mean recipients are only receiving 50 percent of the ration they should. Fuel scarcity has crippled partner logistics, forcing WFP to deploy its own fleet vehicles to keep distributions running.

UNFPA Flash Update #2 on the situation in El Obeid, North Kordofan, Sudan (published 20 July 2026, covering 1-19 July): 21 drone-related incidents were recorded in and around El Obeid between 1-19 July 2026, causing civilian casualties (no aggregate death toll given), damage to critical infrastructure, and further disruption to already-limited essential services, with severe constraints on sexual and reproductive health and gender-based-violence response services due to insecurity and resource shortages.

UN News (24 July 2026), citing a UN Women statement: 'More than half a million people live [in El Obeid], including 83,000 internally displaced people, most of them women and children.' Drone strikes have targeted water points and distribution sites during the day, forcing women and girls to wait until nightfall to collect water, where they face sexual violence instead — UN Women describes this as leaving 'no safe window' to access water. Nationwide, 'drone strikes killed at least 880 civilians in the first four months of 2026 alone — more than 80 per cent of all civilian deaths recorded by the human rights office in that period.' The number of women and girls needing gender-based-violence services nationwide has quadrupled since the conflict began, reaching an estimated 12.7 million in 2026, and cholera is already spreading in Sudan, with 1,330 cases reported by WHO in early July.

published.description: Rapid Support Forces (RSF) paramilitary forces have besieged El Obeid, the capital of North Kordofan state, subjecting the city of more than half a million residents to relentless drone strikes and blockade conditions. Drone strikes have intensified (21 incidents recorded 1-19 July per a UNFPA Flash Update on ReliefWeb, up from 15 strikes over three weeks in the prior UN Human Rights Office count) and the humanitarian situation remains dire: WFP reported more than 120,000 people sheltering in the city's Unified IDP Camp alone (17 July briefing), with food rations cut to 50 percent of full entitlement due to funding shortfalls, while a separate UN News/UN Women report (24 July 2026) put El Obeid's IDP population at 83,000 out of a total city population of more than half a million — a lower figure than the WFP camp count, likely reflecting a different counting methodology or reference date, and not treated here as superseding the more specific WFP camp figure. That 24 July report also describes a 'dual terror' facing women and girls, who face drone strikes if they collect water by day and sexual violence if they wait until night, and cites a nationwide (not El Obeid-specific) figure that drone strikes killed at least 880 civilians across Sudan in the first four months of 2026 alone — more than 80 percent of all civilian deaths recorded by the UN human rights office in that period — plus a UN Women estimate that 12.7 million women and girls nationwide now need gender-based-violence services, having quadrupled since the conflict began. claims.text: GDACS's Volcanic Eruption report for Fuego (Guatemala), updated 05 Aug 2026 08:09 UTC, gives the volcano's coordinates as 14.47°N, -90.88°W, rates the event overall alert level Green, and estimates approximately 1,480,000 people exposed within 30 km and 9,930,000 within 100 km, assessing that the eruption 'is unlikely to require external humanitarian assistance based on the exposed population and coping capacity.'

A Guatemalan Red Cross (Cruz Roja Guatemalteca) / IFRC situation report on ReliefWeb, published 4 August 2026, states that the Fuego eruption began at 08:30 local time on 3 August, that ash-and-gas columns reached 5,000-6,000 m above sea level dispersing more than 40 km to the west, that 9 seismic events generated pyroclastic density currents travelling 5-7 km down the Barranca Seca on the volcano's western flank (posing the greatest threat to communities in San Pedro Yepocapa, Chimaltenango), and that the Guatemalan government established a nationwide orange alert ('alerta anaranjada') to ready shelters and supplies, with CONRED issuing bulletins to authorities and the public.

A follow-up Guatemalan Red Cross / IFRC situation report on ReliefWeb, published 5 August 2026, states the eruption had continued atypically for more than 24 hours since its 3 August 08:30 start, with gas, lava and ash columns of 5,000-7,000 m and pyroclastic density currents of 5-7 km recurring in seven ravines (Seca, Taniluyá, Ceniza, Las Lajas, Honda, Trinidad and El Jute); per CONRED, at least 894 people were sheltered in 3 facilities in Sacatepéquez and Escuintla departments (most from Escuintla), more than 29,000 people were affected, and 'por el momento no se registran daños a personas y viviendas' (no injuries to people or damage to homes had been recorded at that time).

Re-confirmed by direct fetch on 6 August 2026: the Guatemalan Red Cross/IFRC situation report of 5 August 2026 remains the latest, confirming '894 personas se encuentran albergadas en 3 instalaciones... más de 29,000 personas se encuentran afectadas. Por el momento no se registran daños a personas y viviendas' (894 sheltered in 3 facilities; 29,000+ affected; no deaths or housing damage). GDACS's event record (id 1000145) shows Alert Level Green, VEI 4, with no fatality/impact data recorded.

Re-checked 7 August 2026: GDACS's event report (eventid 1000145, updated 5 August 2026 08:09 UTC) still shows an overall Green alert with over 1,700 people evacuated and no deaths or injuries reported; no ReliefWeb or CONRED sitrep newer than the 5 August 2026 Guatemalan Red Cross/IFRC report (894 sheltered, 29,000+ affected, 0 deaths) has been found, though CONRED's 5 August 2026 bulletin ('Tras 50 horas de actividad, Volcan de Fuego retorna a sus parametros normales') indicates the paroxysmal phase has subsided.

Re-checked 8 August 2026: GDACS's volcanic event report (VO 1000145) is byte-identical to the prior check — report timestamp still 5 August 2026 08:09 UTC, Green alert, ~1.48 million people within 30km and ~9.93 million within 100km, VEI 4; no newer GDACS or allowlisted humanitarian report has been published.

OCHA's Latin America & the Caribbean Weekly Situation Update (7 August 2026) states: "Authorities evacuated 1,421 people to five shelters and reported that exposure to ashfall and volcanic hazards has affected more than 29,000 people across 18 communities, particularly Alotenango, the town closest to the volcano... as of 6 August, volcanic activity has begun to decrease from its peak intensity." No deaths are recorded.

Guatemala's disaster coordination agency CONRED declared a nationwide orange alert and evacuated communities in Escuintla and Sacatepéquez departments as the eruption continued for more than 24 hours with no signs of abating. Re-checked 8 August 2026: GDACS's volcanic event report (VO 1000145) is byte-identical to the prior check — report timestamp still 5 August 2026 08:09 UTC, Green alert, ~1.48 million people within 30km and ~9.93 million within 100km, VEI 4; no newer GDACS or allowlisted humanitarian report has been published. claims.text: Sphere India's situation report 'Extreme Weather Events in India — Assam, Odisha, Gujarat, Kerala and Maharashtra' (dated 2 August 2026, posted to ReliefWeb 3 August 2026): 'India is facing multi-state monsoon emergencies across Assam, Odisha, Gujarat, Maharashtra and Kerala, with Assam and Odisha the worst-affected due to severe flooding, large-scale displacement, and extensive crop and livestock losses.' For Assam: 'As per ASDMA's DRIMS report, 1,78,837 people have been impacted' across 7 districts, 20 revenue circles and 349 villages, with 'No human deaths or missing persons... reported as of 1 August 2026.' Statistical overview for Assam: Inmates in Relief Camp 11,489; Non-Camp Inmates in Distribution Centres 5,569; Relief Camps 61; Relief Distribution Centres 17.

Re-checked 9 August 2026: ReliefWeb's India country page shows no Sphere India situation report or IFRC DREF update newer than the previously recorded 2 August/6 August 2026 editions; the combined national figure (at least 84 deaths, at least 320,456 displaced) remains the freshest citable total.

IFRC's Assam Floods DREF Operation report (6 August 2026), hosted on ReliefWeb, states the Assam floods began 19 July 2026 with rainfall reaching up to 490% above normal in parts of Upper Assam; the emergency peaked 27-28 July with more than 800 villages inundated. Since late July, receding river levels and improving weather have led to gradual improvement, though '1,144,733 people remain affected across eight districts, with floodwaters still impacting 437 villages' as of the report date -- a distinct 'affected' metric from this record's previously recorded displacement figure, so it is not used to overwrite that figure. The report characterizes the crisis as having 'moved beyond its peak' while significant humanitarian and recovery needs persist in the worst-affected areas (Charaideo, Sivasagar, Jorhat).

Re-checked 11 August 2026: direct fetch of ReliefWeb's India country page and the IFRC DREF operation report returned HTTP 403 today. A web search surfaced non-allowlisted wire/press reporting (Associated Press, syndicated via NPR member stations and Washington Post) citing the Assam State Disaster Management Authority for an Assam flood death toll of 100 and roughly 300,000 people in relief camps as of 10 August 2026 -- higher than the 74-death IFRC-sourced figure already on file -- but as of this check that figure has not appeared on an allowlisted government, UN, or Red Cross/Red Crescent source, so it is not adopted into the headline totals; the combined confirmed toll (at least 84 deaths, at least 320,456 displaced) remains unchanged.

Sphere India, 'Situation Report 6 -- Extreme Weather Events in India: Assam, Odisha and Kerala' (dated 8 August 2026, posted to ReliefWeb 10 August 2026): Overview -- 'Assam reports 1.55 lakh people affected across 13 districts; Odisha faces one of its largest flood emergencies in recent years with 8.64 lakh people affected across 22 districts.' Assam: 'A total of 464 villages remain inundated, affecting 1,55,849 people... While human casualties remain low, one confirmed death was reported from Charaideo.' Statistical box: Causalities 1 death; Relief Camp inmates 10,326; non-camp 6,881. Odisha: 'Over 8.64 lakh people have been affected across 22 districts... Keonjhar recorded four of the six confirmed deaths.' Statistical box: Causalities 6; Residents evacuated 2.67 lakh; Houses damaged over 1,426. Kerala: 'An unexpected spell of extremely heavy rainfall between 1-7 August triggered severe flooding across Kerala, leaving 26 people dead, 4 missing, and forcing over 27,000 people to take shelter in around 325 relief camps.' Statistical box: Causalities 26 deaths; Missing Persons 4; Relief Camps 325. Gujarat and Maharashtra are outside this report's scope (only Assam, Odisha and Kerala covered).

Re-checked 13 August 2026: Sphere India's Situation Report 6 (8 August 2026) and IFRC's Assam DREF Operation Update No. 1 (6 August 2026) remain the latest editions on ReliefWeb's India flood disaster page; no newer situation report or DREF update has been published. Figures (109 deaths, 347,155 displaced) remain unchanged.

Re-checked 14 August 2026: reliefweb.int returned HTTP 403 to direct fetch; a targeted search confirms Sphere India's Situation Report 6 (8 August 2026) remains the latest edition in its series, with no Situation Report 7 published. Figures (109 deaths, 347,155 displaced) remain unchanged.

GDACS's flood report (event id 1103972, event window 23 June-15 August 2026, updated 16 August 2026) rates the event Green (low impact) with 50 deaths and 69,172 displaced -- a narrower scope centered on Odisha than this record's OCHA-sourced national aggregate -- and flags that a fresh low-pressure area has formed in the Bay of Bengal, with red-level rainfall warnings issued for Odisha and forecasts calling for continued heavy rain through 17-18 August across Himachal Pradesh, Punjab, Haryana and Delhi.

Re-checked 18 August 2026: GDACS's flood report (event id 1103972, episode 23, event window 23 June-15 August 2026) remains Green (low impact) with 50 deaths and 69,172 displaced, unchanged from the 16-17 August checks and still a narrower, Odisha-centered scope than this record's broader national aggregate. reliefweb.int/country/ind again returned HTTP 403 Forbidden to direct fetch. Odisha section: 'Odisha continues to face widespread flooding triggered by a deep depression over the Bay of Bengal, affecting 5.93 lakh+ people across 18 districts... with 2,67,301 lakh people evacuated to safer locations as on 31st July.' Statistical overview: Total Population Affected 5.93 lakh (593,000+); Residents Evacuated to safer location 267,301; Relief Camp and free kitchens operational 600+; Causalities [human]: Not reported. Government Response section: 'State government operating 476 relief camps sheltering 1.76 lakh evacuees across 18 districts.'

Gujarat section: 'Heavy rainfall across south, central, and urban Gujarat has triggered severe flooding, affecting 27,856 people who have been relocated from multiple districts including Surat, Navsari, Bharuch, Tapi, Morbi, Surendranagar, Chhota Udepur, and Vadodara.' Statistical overview: Total Population Affected 27,856 Approx.; Residents Relocated to safer location 22,000 Approx.; Causalities: Not reported. Structural damage includes 'the collapse of a 40-metre stretch of the Tapi riverside road in Surat.'

Kerala section: 'Kerala is experiencing severe monsoon conditions marked by intense rainfall, flash floods, and multiple landslides across high-range districts. As of 2 August 2026, at least 7-8 fatalities have been reported across Kottayam, Idukki, Pathanamthitta, Malappuram and Wayanad... The IMD has issued orange alerts for most districts, and authorities have opened 65 relief camps.' 'Heavy rainfall triggered landslides and flash floods, resulting in 7-8 deaths, including four killed in landslides and three children who drowned in rain-related incidents.' Statistical overview lists Causalities: 7; Total Population Affected: Information awaited.

Maharashtra section: 'Continuous heavy rainfall across Maharashtra has triggered flooding in multiple districts, particularly Nagpur, Palghar, Pune, and parts of the Konkan belt... Landslides in Maval and Mulshi have worsened displacement.' Statistical overview: Total Affected Districts 4; Residents Relocated to safer location: 1,155 Approx.; Causalities: 3.

'The national emergency coordination meeting, convened online by Sphere India's Inter-Agency Coordination Committee on 30 July 2026, brought together national NGOs, UN agencies, the Indian Red Cross Society, Inter-Agency Groups (IAGs), Sphere India members and state-level humanitarian partners to review the escalating flood situation across Assam, Arunachal Pradesh, Gujarat, Maharashtra and Odisha.'

Sphere India's 'Situation Report 2 — Flood Situation in Assam and Mizoram' (dated 18 July 2026, posted to ReliefWeb 19 July 2026): 'Flood conditions continued across Assam on 18 July 2026, with 7 districts affected... A total of 154 villages across 14 revenue circles remain impacted. 21,274 people are affected... No human deaths or missing persons were reported.' This confirms the flooding series began with an earlier Situation Report 1 dated 16 July 2026, establishing the event's onset date.

Re-checked 7 August 2026 via direct fetch of reliefweb.int/country/ind: Sphere India's Situation Report (2 August 2026) remains the latest multi-state coordination sitrep, with no Situation Report #5 published. A separate 5 August 2026 ReliefWeb report by Humanitarian Aid International states, for Assam alone: 'A total of 87 deaths have been confirmed, and more than 705,000 people have been affected' (period '19 July-present') -- this conflicts sharply with the Assam State Disaster Management Authority figure already on file (no deaths, 178,837 affected, as of 1 August) and is not adopted as the headline figure pending corroboration from an official government or UN-coordinated source; it is noted here as a divergent, unverified claim only.

New authoritative report found 8 August 2026: IFRC's DREF Operation Update No. 1 for 'India: Assam Floods' (DREF operation no. MDRIN029, published 6 August 2026 on ReliefWeb) states: "The floods have caused extensive damage to homes, livelihoods, and essential infrastructure across Assam. A total of 1,368 houses were fully damaged and 11,066 partially damaged, while more than 74,450 hectares of agricultural land were affected... In addition, 74 flood-related deaths have been reported... On the basis of situation report shared by Chief Minister Office, as of 28 July 2026, the floods had affected 1,144,733 people across 25 districts... The flooding led to large-scale displacement, with nearly 30,000 people evacuated and over 71,000 people accommodated in relief camps at the height of the emergency." This IFRC figure, sourced to the Assam Chief Minister's Office, is more recent and substantially higher than the ASDMA figure relayed by Sphere India already on file (0 deaths, 178,837 affected, as of 1 August) and is now adopted as the current Assam figure, superseding it; despite the overall decline in flood impacts noted by IFRC, 1,144,733 people remain affected across 8 districts as of this report. Combining updated state figures: Assam 74 deaths / ~30,000 evacuated, Odisha 0 deaths / 267,301 evacuated, Gujarat 0 deaths / ~22,000 relocated, Kerala 7 deaths / evacuee count not reported, Maharashtra 3 deaths / ~1,155 relocated -- giving a revised combined total of at least 84 deaths and at least 320,456 people displaced nationwide. No allowlisted source has declared any state's flooding resolved.

claims.text: A magnitude 7.3 earthquake occurred on 17 July 2026 at 14:48:39 UTC, 58 km WSW of Puerto Madero, Mexico (14.6043N, 92.9517W), at a depth of approximately 18.6 km, in the subduction zone where the Cocos plate converges with North America at the Middle America Trench at approximately 76 mm/yr; the event occurred as reverse (thrust) faulting on or near the plate interface. Two small foreshocks preceded it, including a M4.1 on 14 July and a M4.7 88 minutes prior to the mainshock.

USGS's PAGER system assessed an alert level of Yellow for this earthquake, stating: "The USGS assesses that some damage and fatalities are possible, and that the impact should be relatively localized. Approximately four million people experienced Moderate (MMI V) to Very Strong (MMI VII) shaking." PAGER's probabilistic fatality model places roughly 66% probability on the event causing between 1 and 100 fatalities, and about 27% probability of exceeding 100 fatalities. No revision to this page has occurred since 18 July 2026.

published.description: A magnitude 7.3 earthquake struck offshore southern Mexico on 17 July 2026, in the subduction zone where the Cocos plate thrusts beneath Mexico and Central America at the Middle America Trench. USGS's automated PAGER system assessed a Yellow alert, estimating that roughly four million people experienced moderate to very strong shaking; the agency judged some damage and fatalities possible, though the impact should be relatively localized. One week on, no confirmed casualty toll has been published by any authoritative source, USGS has not revised its event page since 18 July, and no GDACS or ReliefWeb disaster report was ever opened for the event, consistent with a low-severity, non-escalating aftershock sequence.

claims.text: GDACS's flood report for Nepal (event FL 1104091, covering 12 Aug 2026 01:00 UTC to 14 Aug 2026 01:00 UTC) records 11 deaths and 37 displaced people, with an overall Green alert level for low humanitarian impact. The report notes nine road sections across Nepal are impassable due to landslides, road subsidence, and river erosion caused by ongoing heavy monsoon rainfall, with the monsoon bringing widespread cloud cover and moderate rainfall to the Koshi, Bagmati, Karnali, Sudurpashchim, Gandaki and Lumbini provinces.

published.description: Days of heavy monsoon rainfall triggered a series of deadly landslides and flooding across Nepal from around 12 August 2026, concentrated in Rolpa district (Thabang and Sunchhahari rural municipalities) and adjoining Pyuthan district, along with flooding and landslide-related road damage in Koshi, Bagmati, Karnali, Sudurpashchim, Gandaki and Lumbini provinces. GDACS's flood report for Nepal (event 1104091, covering 12-14 August 2026) recorded 11 deaths and 37 displaced people, assessed at an overall Green (low humanitarian impact) alert level, and noted nine road sections across the country were impassable due to landslides, road subsidence and river erosion caused by the ongoing monsoon. The largest single incident buried houses at Kotalbara settlement in Thabang Rural Municipality-5, Rolpa, on the night of 12-13 August; Nepali authorities and media reported the confirmed toll from that and a second landslide at Phalbang, Sunchhahari Rural Municipality-2, continuing to rise over subsequent days as search teams recovered bodies in neighbouring Pyuthan district, with local reporting (not yet corroborated by an allowlisted source) putting the combined toll as high as the mid-teens and several people still missing.

claims.text: USGS recorded a magnitude 5.5 earthquake on 19 July 2026 at 02:24:35 UTC, 4 km SSW of Chupaca, Peru, at a depth of about 10 km, with a PAGER alert level of Yellow ("some casualties and damage are possible and the impact should be relatively localized").

published.description: USGS recorded a magnitude 5.5 earthquake on 19 July 2026 at 02:24:35 UTC, 4 km SSW of Chupaca in Peru's Andean Junín Region, at a shallow depth of about 10 km. USGS's PAGER system assessed a Yellow alert level, indicating that some casualties and localized damage were possible given the shallow depth and the region's vulnerable construction. The quake drew sustained top-tier international coverage (Al Jazeera, Bloomberg, Euronews) reporting several deaths, dozens of injuries, and damage to homes and hospital buildings in and around the regional capital Huancayo, but no allowlisted authoritative source (USGS, ReliefWeb, GDACS) has published a confirmed casualty, injury, or damage figure; no GDACS or ReliefWeb disaster report was opened for this event. published.description: Multiple simultaneous wildfires broke out southwest of Madrid and in neighbouring Ávila province, Spain, on 22 July 2026 amid extreme heat and strong winds, prompting evacuations in towns including Villa del Prado, San Martín de Valdeiglesias, Pelayos de la Presa and Aldea del Fresno. GDACS escalated its alert from Green to Orange as of episode 19 (27 July 2026); as of episode 22 (30 July 2026) the burned area stood at about 66,098 hectares with roughly 20,200 people in the fire-affected area. No newer GDACS episode has been published and no thermal-anomaly detection has been recorded since 30 July 2026, indicating the fire is now contained. Spain's Interior Ministry declared a national emergency for the fires on 23-24 July 2026 — widely reported as the first such declaration linked to a wildfire — and evacuation figures well above 10,000 people have been widely reported; neither the national-emergency declaration nor the evacuation count has been confirmed by an allowlisted authoritative source.

impact.summary: GDACS's event report (eventid 1029643, episode 22) keeps this forest fire in Spain at an Overall Orange alert for medium humanitarian impact, citing 66,098 hectares burned and 20,200 people in the fire-affected area, with the most recent thermal-anomaly detection on 30 July 2026. Re-checked 4 August 2026: GDACS still shows episode 22 as the current/latest episode, with figures unchanged and no thermal-anomaly detection since 30 July — five days with no new hotspot activity — indicating the fire is now contained. No allowlisted authoritative source has yet published a confirmed death toll or official evacuation count for this fire; Spain's widely reported national emergency declaration (23-24 July) and evacuation figures above 10,000 people come from non-allowlisted media and have not been independently confirmed here.

published.description: Heavy monsoon rainfall triggered flooding and landslides across Sri Lanka's central highlands beginning around 2 August 2026, affecting Kandy, Nuwara Eliya, Kegalle and Ratnapura districts, with the town of Hatton (Nuwara Eliya District) singled out for a fatal landslide. claims.text: WHO Representative to Sudan Dr. Shible Sahbani reported more than 1,330 confirmed cholera cases and 114 confirmed deaths, a case fatality rate of 13.7 percent, in an outbreak affecting several states, mainly in the western part of the country, the Darfurs and the Kordofans, briefing journalists in Geneva on 10 July 2026. Aid officials say the true number of fatalities is likely much higher, and the disease is expected to spread further as the rainy season sets in, particularly among people who have fled towns and rural areas in North Kordofan.

Re-checked 8 August 2026: ECDC's cholera-monthly page still shows Sudan's most recent data cut as 12 July 2026 (1,511 cases, 153 deaths since 1 January 2026); no newer monthly update has been published for the current (27 June 2026-onward) outbreak.

ECDC's cholera worldwide monthly overview and its Weekly Communicable Disease Threats Report (Week 33, 8-14 Aug 2026) both confirm the Sudan cholera dataset has not been refreshed since a data cut of 12 July 2026: 1,511 cumulative cases and 153 deaths reported since 1 January 2026, ranking Sudan second globally after DRC (3,841 cases). WHO/EMRO's dedicated Sudan crisis page returned repeated server errors (HTTP 502) and could not be verified this session.

Re-checked 18 August 2026: ECDC's cholera-monthly page (still dated 27 July 2026) continues to report, for Sudan, 1,511 cumulative cases including 153 deaths since 1 January 2026 as of the 12 July 2026 data cut -- unchanged from the prior check; WHO/EMRO's Sudan crisis page returned a server error (HTTP 502) again this session, and reliefweb.int/country/sdn returned HTTP 403; no newer WHO or ReliefWeb figure was found.

UN News report (14 July 2026), citing OCHA, reconfirms WHO's count of 1,330 confirmed cholera cases and 114 deaths as of 7 July 2026, and describes the outbreak's continued spread: new confirmed and suspected cases in Kalma/Kampala displacement camp (South Darfur) and Tawila (North Darfur); West Kordofan reporting the highest caseload with new suspected cases and deaths; and North Kordofan reporting 32 new suspected cases in Gharb Bara locality in a single day. WHO delivered 8.5 tonnes of medical supplies to Kadugli and Dilling, South Kordofan — its first shipment there since December 2024 — and UNICEF delivered health supplies to El Fula, West Kordofan, serving about 429,000 people.

WFP report (data as of 17 July 2026): regular power outages are disrupting water supplies in El Obeid, and more than 30 new cholera cases have been recorded there as the city's displacement and hunger crisis deepens.

UN Women statement (24 July 2026): 'Cholera is already spreading in Sudan, with 1,330 cases reported by WHO in early July,' confirming no revised national cumulative total has superseded the 7 July WHO count as of this date.

Re-checked 1 August 2026: no newer WHO or ReliefWeb figure supersedes the 10 July 2026 Geneva briefing count of 1,330+ confirmed cholera cases and 114 deaths (CFR 13.7%) in Sudan reported by WHO's Representative to Sudan; WHO's global multi-country cholera epidemiological update series has not published a newer Sudan-specific count as of this check.

This multi-country surveillance figure is dated to 31 May 2026 and is superseded chronologically by the 1,330-case/114-death figure WHO's Representative to Sudan reported on 10 July 2026 for the same national outbreak; re-checked 5 August 2026, no WHO or ReliefWeb Sudan-specific update newer than the 10 July figure has been published, and no allowlisted source has declared the outbreak contained.

published.description: Sudan's third cholera wave in as many years has spread across war-affected western and central states, principally Darfur and Kordofan, where conflict and constrained humanitarian access are hampering the response. WHO warns the outbreak could worsen further as the rainy season sets in and displacement continues around besieged cities such as El Obeid, where WFP reported more than 30 additional cases in mid-July. ECDC's cholera-monthly surveillance page (updated 27 July 2026, data as of 12 July 2026) now records a higher national cumulative total of 1,511 cases and 153 deaths since 1 January 2026 (CFR ~10.1%), superseding the WHO Representative to Sudan's 10 July briefing figure (1,330 cases, 114 deaths, CFR 13.7%) as the most current confirmed national aggregate. Continued geographic spread has been reported into new localities in North and West Kordofan and South Darfur. A separate, earlier WHO multi-country cholera epidemiological update (data as of 31 May 2026, published 30 June) recorded a lower cumulative Sudan figure of 527 cases and 61 deaths for 1 January-31 May 2026 under its own multi-country surveillance stream; that update predates and does not supersede the more recent figures. published.description: A tropical disturbance east-southeast of the Marianas organized into Tropical Depression 09W on 1 July 2026 and was named Bavi as a tropical storm on 2 July. Bavi underwent rapid intensification and reached Category 5 super typhoon strength by 4 July with sustained winds near 287 km/h, prompting GDACS to issue an overall Red alert as the storm tracked through Guam and the Northern Mariana Islands. After passing near Rota, the storm continued west, entering the Philippine Area of Responsibility on 8 July (locally named Inday), tracked across Taiwan and Japan's Ryukyu Islands, and made landfall in Zhejiang Province, eastern China, on 11 July before weakening over land.

impact.summary: Super Typhoon Bavi (locally named Inday in the Philippines) made landfall in Zhejiang Province, eastern China, at 23:20 local time on 11 July 2026, after peaking at Category 5 strength (287 km/h sustained winds) near Guam and the Northern Mariana Islands on 4-6 July. GDACS's event report (current as of 12 July 2026) keeps the overall alert at Red for an event window of 01 Jul 2026 00:00 UTC to 11 Jul 2026 18:00 UTC, with a population of 35.3 million exposed to Category 1 (120 km/h) or higher winds; the current alert's urgency status is now 'Past', consistent with the storm weakening after landfall. GDACS's report does not list a confirmed fatality count for the event; Philippine media reported at least 18-19 deaths from landslides and heavy rain on Mindanao, and China evacuated more than 1.7 million people in Zhejiang ahead of landfall, though neither figure comes from an allowlisted authoritative source.

claims.text: NOAA's Central Pacific Hurricane Center advisory (11 PM HST, 15 August 2026): Hurricane Lala had maximum sustained winds of 75 mph (120 km/h) and a minimum central pressure of 988 mb, located near latitude 19.6N, longitude 157.0W, about 65 miles west of Kailua-Kona and 130 miles south-southeast of Honolulu, moving northwest at 15 mph with gradual weakening expected Sunday. Forecast rainfall totals were 4-8 inches for the Big Island and windward Maui with a storm-total maximum of 30-35 inches over windward Hawaii Island, and 4-6 inches (maximum 8 inches) for the remaining islands, with 1-3 feet of storm surge; the advisory warned these amounts 'will produce life-threatening flooding and mudslides, especially in areas of steep terrain.'

GDACS tropical cyclone report for ONE-C-26/Lala (episode 23, reporting window 12 Aug 2026 15:00 UTC - 18 Aug 2026 03:00 UTC): overall Green alert (low humanitarian impact) with maximum sustained winds of 148 km/h (Category 1) and an affected population of approximately 10,000 people in Category 1 or higher wind zones, both consistent with the prior report; the primary GDACS event assessment records no deaths or damage figures (a separate media-headlines module on the same page cites third-party news reports of one storm-related death and up to ~111,000 customers without power on Hawaii Island, which are not GDACS's own assessed figures).

Emergency Proclamation Relating to Tropical Storm Lala, signed 14 August 2026 by C. Kimo Alameda, Ph.D., Mayor of the County of Hawaiʻi, under Hawaii Revised Statutes Chapter 127A, declaring a local state of emergency for Hawaiʻi County citing NWS forecasts of winds of 74-110 mph, rainfall of 8-12 inches (10-15 inches over windward areas), storm surge of 1-3 feet, and surf heights of 15-20 feet, with potential for 'considerable damage, downed trees and power lines, and power and communications disruptions.'

claims.source_name: Office of the Governor of Hawaiʻi
claims.text: Governor Josh Green signed a statewide emergency proclamation on 13 August 2026 ahead of Tropical Storm Lala, mobilizing state agency personnel, equipment and resources; the Hawaiʻi National Guard was prepared to support response efforts. A follow-up state update (16 August) reports approximately 180 Hawaiʻi National Guard personnel positioned statewide, including a 41-member Task Force Hawaiʻi and a 19-member Task Force Maui, and confirms the Hawaiʻi Department of Transportation closed Hilo International Airport (ITO) and Ellison Onizuka Kona International Airport (KOA) at 2 p.m., with Hawaiʻi Island and Maui County commercial ports also closed to all terminal, facility and vessel operations absent US Coast Guard approval.

GDACS tracked the storm as Central Pacific tropical cyclone ONE-C-26, active 12-16 August 2026, rating it a Green alert (low humanitarian impact) with maximum sustained winds of 130 km/h (Category 1), an estimated 10,000 people affected by Category 1 or higher wind speeds, a maximum storm surge of 0.2 m, and 'low' vulnerability assessed for the United States.

NOAA's Central Pacific Hurricane Center Advisory Number 20 (11 PM HST, 16 August 2026): Tropical Storm Lala located near 20.7N 162.6W, about 305 miles west of Honolulu and 225 miles west-southwest of Lihue, with maximum sustained winds of 60 mph (95 km/h) and a minimum central pressure of 997 mb, moving westward at 13 mph. 'There are no coastal watches or warnings in effect.' Lala is forecast to become a hurricane again by Wednesday while continuing to move westward away from the main Hawaiian Islands.

County of Hawaiʻi update (posted 16 August 2026, 7:37 PM): all non-emergency County operations suspended Monday, 17 August, following Hurricane Lala's impact on the island; 'record-breaking' power outages reported (no specific figure given), multiple road closures documented on the County's Hazard Impact Map, 43 people sheltering at two emergency shelters (Nāʻālehu Elementary School and Robert N. Herkes Gym), search-and-rescue operations ongoing in Nāʻālehu, Waiʻōhinu and Pāhala, and an island-wide 'Essential Only' water-conservation request.

GDACS tropical cyclone report for ONE-C-26 (episode 20, reporting window 12 Aug 2026 15:00 UTC - 17 Aug 2026 09:00 UTC): overall Green alert (low humanitarian impact); maximum sustained winds 139 km/h (Category 1), up from 130 km/h in the prior report; affected population approximately 10,000 people in Category 1 or higher wind zones, unchanged.

County of Hawaiʻi flash-flooding update (16 August 2026, 1:07 AM): the County coordinated search-and-rescue operations in Nāʻālehu and Waiʻōhinu in Kaʻū after severe flash flooding cut off road access and inundated homes; National Guard high-water vehicles and a US Coast Guard helicopter assisted, and rescued residents were transported to Robert N. Herkes Gym in Pāhala and the Public Works base yard. Mayor Kimo Alameda: 'Our highest priority is the safety of our residents.'

NOAA's Central Pacific Hurricane Center Advisory Number 24 (11 PM HST, 17 August 2026): Hurricane Lala re-strengthened to a hurricane, located near 20.4N 166.1W, about 440 miles southeast of Maro Reef, with maximum sustained winds near 80 mph (130 km/h), higher gusts, and a minimum central pressure of 985 mb, moving toward the west near 10 mph. Hurricane-force winds extend outward up to 15 miles from the center and tropical-storm-force winds up to 90 miles. 'There are no coastal watches or warnings in effect,' though interests in the Papahanaumokuakea Marine National Monument were advised to monitor Lala's progress as watches would likely be needed early Tuesday. Additional strengthening was forecast during the next day or so, with the system expected to remain a hurricane for several days, moving west through Tuesday before turning northwest and then north by Thursday -- continuing to track away from the main Hawaiian Islands.

published.description: Hurricane Lala strengthened to a Category 1 hurricane as it passed close to Hawaii Island on 15-16 August 2026, prompting a Hawaii County emergency proclamation (14 August, Mayor C. Kimo Alameda) and a statewide emergency proclamation (13 August, Governor Josh Green) ahead of the storm's approach. NOAA's Central Pacific Hurricane Center's 11 PM HST advisory on 15 August put Lala's maximum sustained winds at 75 mph with a central pressure of 988 mb, located about 65 miles west of Kailua-Kona and moving northwest at 15 mph, with forecast rainfall of up to 30-35 inches over windward Hawaii Island and warnings of life-threatening flash flooding and mudslides. A Hurricane Warning was in effect for Hawaii County and a Tropical Storm Warning for Maui, Oahu and Kauai counties. The State of Hawaiʻi activated approximately 180 National Guard personnel statewide, closed Hilo International Airport and Kona International Airport, and closed Hawaiʻi Island and Maui County commercial ports, while GDACS separately tracked the storm (as Central Pacific system ONE-C-26) as a Green/low-impact Category 1 system affecting an estimated 10,000 people. No death toll, injury count, or displacement figure has been confirmed via an allowlisted government or NOAA source as of this record. Re-checked 17 August 2026: Lala passed closest to Hawaii Island on 15-16 August, then weakened; NOAA's Central Pacific Hurricane Center Advisory 20 (11 PM HST, 16 August) put it as a tropical storm with 60 mph sustained winds and a 997 mb central pressure at 20.7N 162.6W (about 305 miles west of Honolulu), moving westward at 13 mph away from the main Hawaiian Islands, with no coastal watches or warnings in effect, though NOAA forecasts Lala could re-strengthen into a hurricane by Wednesday as it continues moving away. GDACS's tropical cyclone report (episode 20, window 12-17 August 2026) recorded a peak of 139 km/h sustained winds (up from 130 km/h) with the affected-population estimate unchanged at about 10,000. The County of Hawaiʻi's 16 August 7:37 PM update reports 'record-breaking' power outages (no county-published figure), multiple road closures, and 43 people sheltering at two emergency shelters (Nāʻālehu Elementary School and Robert N. Herkes Gym), with search-and-rescue operations ongoing in Nāʻālehu, Waiʻōhinu and Pāhala after flash flooding cut off road access in those communities on 16 August, and all non-emergency County operations suspended 17 August; an island-wide 'Essential Only' water-conservation notice was issued by the County Department of Water Supply due to storm-caused outages affecting water-system operations. No allowlisted government or NOAA source has published a confirmed death toll, injury count, quantified power-outage figure, or displacement total as of this re-check; unofficial media reports describe an unconfirmed storm-related fatality near South Point under investigation, but no allowlisted source was fetchable to verify it. Re-checked 18 August 2026: NOAA's Central Pacific Hurricane Center Advisory 24 (11 PM HST, 17 August) reports Lala re-strengthened into a hurricane -- 80 mph sustained winds, 985 mb central pressure, located about 440 miles southeast of Maro Reef and continuing to move west/northwest away from the main Hawaiian Islands, with no coastal watches or warnings in effect and additional strengthening forecast. GDACS's tropical cyclone report (episode 23) records unchanged Green/low-impact status with about 10,000 people in Category 1-or-higher wind zones; GDACS's own event assessment carries no death or damage figures, though a media-headlines module on the same GDACS page cites third-party news reports of one storm-related death (a woman in Naalehu) and roughly 100,000-126,000 power customers still affected on Hawaii Island. Both the Office of the Governor of Hawaii (governor.hawaii.gov) and the County of Hawaii (hawaiicounty.gov) returned HTTP 403 Forbidden on every page fetched this session, so no allowlisted government source could be used to confirm a death toll, injury count, power-outage figure, or damage total as of this re-check; the impact fields therefore remain unconfirmed pending a successful fetch of an official state or county source.

claims.source_name: Office of the Governor of Nevada
claims.text: Governor Joe Lombardo declared a state of emergency, effective August 10 and remaining in effect through August 17, 2026 unless terminated sooner, for areas of Washoe County and the Reno-Sparks Indian Colony impacted by the Bug and Fred Mountain Fires; as of that evening the fires had burned more than 16,000 acres and more than 6,000 people had been evacuated, with thousands more residents in warning zones. The declaration directs all state agencies to work through the Nevada Emergency Operations Center to supplement local efforts, and the Federal Emergency Management Agency separately authorized the use of federal funds to assist Nevada in combating the Bug Fire.

As of 8/14/2026: Bug Fire 88,422 acres, 31% contained, started 8 August 2026 at 3:30 PM, 591 personnel assigned; Stallion Fire 40,698 acres, 44% contained, started 10 August 2026, 322 personnel assigned; combined 93,367 acres and 717 personnel. Location given as 3 miles south of Hallelujah Junction, California. Both fires are attributed to human causes, burning in tall grass, brush and pinyon-juniper fuels. The 14 August 2026 update notes: "Wetting Rains Aid Firefighting Resources Increasing Containment," with thunderstorms bringing cooler temperatures and higher humidity.

InciWeb (update posted 15 August 2026, 7:49 PM): Bug Fire is 93,381 acres and 58% contained (717 personnel); Stallion Fire is 40,691 acres and 81% contained (282 personnel); combined-incident totals are 94,105 acres and 84% of the perimeter contained, with 849 total personnel assigned. No deaths, injuries or structures-destroyed figures are listed.

published.description: The Bug Fire ignited on 8 August 2026 near Hallelujah Junction on the California-Nevada border and, driven by strong winds and dry vegetation, grew rapidly into Washoe County, Nevada, threatening communities including Cold Springs and the Reno-Sparks Indian Colony; the neighboring Stallion Fire ignited nearby on 10 August 2026. On 10 August 2026, Nevada Governor Joe Lombardo declared a state of emergency for areas of Washoe County and the Reno-Sparks Indian Colony impacted by the Bug and (adjoining) Fred Mountain Fires, citing more than 16,000 acres burned at that time and more than 6,000 people evacuated, directing all state agencies to work through the Nevada Emergency Operations Center to supplement local efforts; the declaration remains in effect through 17 August 2026 unless terminated sooner. InciWeb's joint Bug & Stallion Fire incident page reports that, as of 14 August 2026, the Bug Fire had grown to 88,422 acres (31% contained) and the Stallion Fire to 40,698 acres (44% contained) — a combined 93,367 acres and 717 personnel assigned — with both fires attributed to human causes and burning in grass, brush and pinyon-juniper fuels; an update that day noted wetting rains aiding containment gains with cooler, more humid conditions. No allowlisted source has yet published a confirmed statewide death toll, injury count, or structure-loss figure for the combined incident, and no source has declared the fires contained. Re-checked 16 August 2026: containment has continued to advance -- Bug Fire remains 93,381 acres at 58% contained while Stallion Fire has grown very slightly to 40,691 acres but reached 81% contained; the combined incident is now 94,105 acres and 84% of the perimeter contained. Status upgraded to contained given the high combined containment level, though Bug Fire's 58% still represents a substantial uncontained perimeter warranting continued monitoring.

impact.summary: Nevada Governor Joe Lombardo's 10 August 2026 state-of-emergency declaration reported more than 16,000 acres burned and more than 6,000 people evacuated from areas of Washoe County and the Reno-Sparks Indian Colony at that time, with thousands more residents in warning zones. InciWeb's incident page for the merged Bug & Stallion Fire complex shows the fires had grown substantially since then, to a combined 93,367 acres (88,422 ac Bug Fire at 31% containment; 40,698 ac Stallion Fire at 44% containment) as of 14 August 2026, with 717 personnel assigned; no allowlisted source has yet published an updated statewide evacuation count, confirmed death toll, or structure-loss figure beyond the governor's initial declaration. No source has declared the fires contained. Re-checked 16 August 2026: combined incident now 94,105 acres, 84% contained (Bug 58%, Stallion 81%); status upgraded to contained.

The fires have degraded air quality and caused evacuations of tens of thousands of people across Washington and Idaho."

claims.text: Washington Governor Ferguson's statewide wildfire emergency proclamation (1 August 2026) states 'over 1,000 fires have burned approximately 425,000 acres statewide -- the highest acreage since 2021,' with 200,000+ acres actively burning across 12 large fires; a federal emergency declaration approved 4 August 2026 covers Chelan, Ferry, Okanogan, Spokane, Stevens and Yakima counties plus the Yakama Nation, Colville Reservation and Spokane Tribe of Indians, with 110 Washington National Guard members activated and 13 State Fire Marshal task forces mobilized.

InciWeb Sinlahekin Fire incident page, updated 16 August 2026, 10:41 p.m. PT: the fire holds at 152,682 acres (unchanged from 15 August) with containment up to 44% (from 42%) and 1,736 personnel assigned (up from 1,677), estimated full-containment date still 19 August 2026; InciWeb notes 'light, lingering heat remains in select areas of the incident where heavy dead and down fuels continue to burn.'

InciWeb Sinlahekin Fire incident page, updated 17 August 2026, 10:45 p.m. PT: the fire has grown to 153,843 acres (up from 152,682 acres on 16 August) with containment holding at 44% and 1,731 personnel assigned (down from 1,736), estimated full-containment date still 19 August 2026; the page continues to note light, lingering heat in select areas where heavy dead-and-down fuels continue to burn.

claims.source_name: Office of the Governor of Washington State
claims.text: Office of the Governor of Washington State (4 August 2026): announces that President Trump approved a federal emergency declaration for Washington's wildfires, covering Chelan, Ferry, Okanogan, Spokane, Stevens and Yakima counties and the Confederated Tribes and Bands of the Yakama Nation, the Confederated Tribes of the Colville Reservation, and the Spokane Tribe of Indians; Governor Ferguson: "The declaration allows our federal partners to mobilize their resources and personnel to support our response, and unlocks resources for state, local and tribal governments," including support for "evacuating and providing emergency shelters for people who are displaced by the wildfires," "emergency food and water, search and rescue operations and more." This followed Governor Ferguson's own statewide wildfire emergency proclamation of 1 August 2026. No casualty, structure-loss, or acreage figures are given in this release.
